newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland offers Vietnam $70 million shipyard credit.
newsitem.headline: Poland offers Vietnam $70 million shipyard credit.

text.p: Poland's Solidarity union, battling to save the bankrupt Gdansk shipyard, on Wednesday denounced a Polish government offer to provide $70 million in credits to Vietnam for modernisation of its Ha Long shipyard.
Polish Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz proposed the government credit to his counterpart Vo Van Kiet on Tuesday at the start of a two-day visit by the Vietnamese premier.

"In view of our shipbuilding industries' difficulties, including those of the Gdansk yard, Premier Cimoszewicz's initiative bears the hallmarks of economic sabotage," the union's Gdansk region leadership said in a statement.

PAP news agency reported the statement as saying the offer amounted to "supporting competitors on the world shipbuilding market at the cost to the domestic industry of a sum which could restructure our yards so that they could rival world standards."
Cimoszewicz rejected Solidarity's argument as absurd and said the move was designed to promote Polish exports.

"This is a credit which will allow Polish construction firms and companies specialised in manufacturing shipyard equipment to gain a marketplace to export their goods, work and expertise," PAP quoted him as telling reporters.
According to a Polish government statement, Kiet offered preferential treatment for Polish machinery and equipment.
Vietnam also wants Polish participation in modernising such sectors as coal and copper mines, chemicals and food processing.

Before the 1989 fall of communism in Poland, Warsaw gave Vietnam extensive grant aid and built or equipped Ha Long as well as about 20 other projects such as a railyard and coal mine. But economic exchanges have since slumped.
Cimoszewicz, a former communist turned pro-market social democrat, briefed his communist guest on Poland's economic achievements since the fall of the old system.
Kiet, 74, is visiting Poland, the Czech republic, Italy and Hungary between May 20 and 28 in a bid to revitalise ties with Vietnam's Central European former partners.

The Gdansk shipyard has signed a contract to build three ships, each worth $27.5 million, for a German-owned firm, reawakening hopes for reviving the enterprise where Solidarity was born 17 years ago in defiance of communism.

The deal still awaits a final agreement on financing and the union bitterly condemns the government led by ex-communists for not providing government guarantees for credits, saying this decision was made out of political spite.
